description: We are a multidisciplinary crew of aspiring engineers and innovators, bringing together expertise in Aerospace, Chemical, and Mechanical Engineering, as well as Computer Science. Like a spacecraft crew, each of us has a different specialty, but we share one mission: advancing technology for safer and more sustainable human space exploration. Combining our knowledge and skills, we set out to explore how technology can help astronauts better understand and monitor their health beyond Earth.
summary: TanawOrbit is an astronaut health-monitoring and self-assessment prototype designed to demonstrate how personalized health tracking can support astronaut well-being during long-duration space missions. It integrates physiological measurements, behavioral assessments, sleep and fatigue monitoring, nutritional tracking, and physical performance assessments into one accessible platform. Using synthetic astronaut health data, the system organizes historical records, compares measurements against individual baselines, and visualizes parameter-specific trends to help users recognize changes over time. By combining multidomain monitoring with NASA-informed health references and educational guidance, TanawOrbit explores an approach to understanding astronaut health that goes beyond isolated measurements and generalized reference ranges. Rather than providing medical diagnoses, it promotes health awareness and informed self-assessment, demonstrating the potential of personalized digital monitoring to support human health during future space exploration.
details:
TanawOrbit's Project Solution

What happens when astronauts venture farther from Earth, where medical assistance is no longer just a call away?

TanawOrbit is an interactive astronaut health and mission-monitoring web application designed to collect, track, and analyze personalized health data alongside relevant spacecraft environmental conditions.

The platform brings together physiological health monitoring, behavioral assessments, nutritional tracking, physical performance analysis, and mission environmental information in one integrated interface. By combining historical records, individual baseline comparisons, and scientific references, TanawOrbit transforms health measurements into understandable trends, monitoring observations, and educational guidance.

How Does Our Solution Work?

TanawOrbit follows a data-driven monitoring workflow that transforms collected information into meaningful observations.

  1. Data Collection: Astronauts enter health measurements, complete self-assessments, and record relevant activities through the application.
  2. Data Validation: Submitted measurements are checked against defined input requirements, units, and validation criteria.
  3. Historical Data Processing: The system organizes and retrieves previous records to establish an astronaut's monitoring history.
  4. Personal Baseline Comparison: Current measurements are compared against individual historical baselines to identify numerical changes.
  5. Trend Analysis: Historical records are processed using parameter-specific calculations and presented through appropriate visualizations.
  6. Environmental Monitoring: Selected orbital and spacecraft environmental parameters are evaluated against their corresponding reference information.
  7. Monitoring Observations and Guidance: Results are presented through understandable interpretations and NASA-informed educational content.

Health and Mission-Monitoring Features

1. Cardiovascular Health and Vital Signs

The application monitors essential physiological indicators to help track changes in an astronaut's condition.

  • Heart Rate: Resting heart-rate measurements (BPM).
  • Blood Pressure: Systolic and diastolic readings (mmHg).
  • Body Temperature: Recorded body temperature (°C).
  • Oxygen Saturation: Peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂, %).

Measurements are organized into historical records and interpreted using configured reference information and measurement context.

2. Sleep and Circadian Rhythm

Sleep monitoring helps astronauts understand changes in their rest patterns and daily schedules.

The application includes:

  • Sleep duration calculated from recorded sleep and wake-up times.
  • Sleep schedule consistency through bedtime and wake-up deviations.
  • Self-reported fatigue levels using a 1–5 scale.
  • Rolling seven-day sleep-duration averages.

These measurements help illustrate changes in sleep patterns and fatigue over time.

3. Behavioral Health

Recognizing the psychological demands of long-duration missions, TanawOrbit includes a self-reported mood-monitoring feature.

Astronauts can record daily mood selections, which are organized into a mood calendar and weekly frequency chart. This allows users to review their reported emotional patterns over time.

4. Nutrition and Supplements

Maintaining adequate nutrition is an important consideration during space missions. TanawOrbit incorporates a nutritional tracking system supported by a space-food database.

Astronauts can view their food consumption and review estimated nutritional contributions, including:

  • Daily calorie intake (kcal).
  • Protein intake (g).
  • Carbohydrate intake (g).
  • Fat intake (g).
  • Blood glucose readings (mg/dL), with fasting or non-fasting context.

5. Musculoskeletal Health

Physical activity is an important component of maintaining astronaut health during missions. TanawOrbit includes an exercise-tracking feature that records daily exercise duration and presents activity history against a configured daily target.

6. Sensorimotor Performance

TanawOrbit explores interactive assessments of coordination and response performance through two activities:

  • Hand-Eye Coordination: An interactive target-tapping task that records accuracy and completion time.
  • Visual Reaction Time: A fast-reading assessment that records reaction-time results.

These activities demonstrate how interactive tasks can be used to collect performance-related measurements and track changes across assessments.

7. Dynamic Orbital Conditions

Beyond individual health measurements, TanawOrbit incorporates selected parameters describing the spacecraft's position and surrounding space environment.

The module includes:

  • Orbital Position: Latitude and longitude coordinates.
  • Orbital Altitude: Spacecraft elevation above Earth's reference surface (km).
  • Space Radiation Exposure: Radiation dose rate (µGy/h).
  • Gravitational Environment: Microgravity measurements (µg).

These parameters provide additional mission context and demonstrate how environmental information can complement astronaut health monitoring.

8. Cabin Internal Conditions

TanawOrbit also incorporates reference information about spacecraft characteristics and internal environmental conditions, using the International Space Station (ISS) as a reference.

These include:

  • Physical Characteristics: Station dimensions, mass, habitable volume, and power generation.
  • Crew and Orbital Information: Nominal crew complement, orbital inclination, altitude, period, and velocity.
  • Atmospheric Conditions: Cabin pressure and oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen partial pressures.
  • Thermal Conditions: Cabin temperature and dew point.
  • Air Circulation: Ventilation velocity.
  • Air Quality: Particulate and trace chemical concentrations.

This module provides environmental reference information to help contextualize the conditions in which astronauts operate.

Personalized Health Monitoring and Trend Analysis

One of TanawOrbit's central features is its emphasis on individual health patterns rather than relying exclusively on generalized population reference ranges. The application compares current measurements against an astronaut's historical records to identify changes relative to their established personal baseline. For example, an increase in resting heart rate may be highlighted even when the latest measurement remains within a general adult reference range.

Different parameters also use appropriate analytical approaches, including daily averages, rolling seven-day averages, schedule deviations, symptom frequencies, and assessment performance records. These calculations allow measurements to be understood over time rather than treated as isolated readings.

NASA-Informed Educational Guidance

TanawOrbit incorporates NASA publications, technical standards, and scientific literature to establish the research foundation for its monitoring parameters. The application distinguishes between recorded measurements, calculated changes, configured reference ranges, and research-informed explanations. This approach promotes scientific awareness while avoiding unsupported medical diagnoses or treatment recommendations. TanawOrbit is an educational proof of concept and does not replace flight surgeons or established crew medical procedures.

What Makes TanawOrbit Creative?

TanawOrbit explores a broader approach to astronaut monitoring by bringing multiple dimensions of health and mission information into one interactive platform.

Its creative contributions include:

  • Personalized Monitoring: Comparing current measurements against individual historical baselines rather than relying exclusively on generalized reference values.
  • Multidomain Integration: Connecting physiological, behavioral, nutritional, physical-performance, and environmental information within one platform.
  • Interactive Performance Assessments: Incorporating target-tapping and visual reaction-time activities to demonstrate sensorimotor monitoring.
  • Spaceflight-Oriented Context: Including orbital and spacecraft environmental information alongside individual health records.
  • Research-Informed Interpretation: Connecting monitoring parameters with NASA resources and scientific literature to make health information more understandable.

Rather than presenting isolated measurements, TanawOrbit demonstrates how different types of information can contribute to a more comprehensive picture of astronaut health and mission conditions.

Factors Considered in Development

Several scientific, technical, and operational considerations guided the development of TanawOrbit:

  • Scientific Validity: Health indicators, measurement definitions, units, and calculations were reviewed against available scientific literature and NASA resources.
  • Spaceflight Relevance: Monitoring parameters were selected based on their relationship to human health, performance, and the spaceflight environment.
  • Individual Differences: Personal baseline comparisons were incorporated to recognize that astronauts may have different historical health patterns.
  • Measurement Context: Factors such as resting versus post-activity heart rate and fasting versus non-fasting glucose measurements were considered when interpreting data.
  • Data Privacy: Fictional astronaut profiles and synthetic health measurements are used for demonstration.
  • Usability: Monitoring information and visualizations were designed to make complex measurements easier to understand.
  • Scientific and Medical Limitations: General reference ranges are not presented as validated astronaut-specific diagnostic thresholds, and the application does not replace professional medical assessment.

Benefits and Intended Impact

TanawOrbit aims to contribute to astronaut health awareness and future human space exploration by:

  • Demonstrating personalized monitoring through individual historical baselines.
  • Making physiological, behavioral, and performance trends easier to understand.
  • Supporting nutritional, physical activity, and women's health tracking.
  • Connecting health measurements with relevant NASA research.
  • Exploring how mission environmental information can complement health monitoring.
  • Demonstrating accessible digital technologies that could inform future astronaut health-monitoring and decision-support systems.

Ultimately, TanawOrbit aims to demonstrate how integrated, personalized monitoring can support a better understanding of astronaut health during long-duration space missions.

Tools and Technologies Used

Frontend Development and Interface Design

  • React.js (v19) – Frontend framework for developing interactive and reusable user-interface components.
  • TypeScript (v5.7) – Type-safe programming language used for frontend and backend application logic.
  • Vite (v8) – Frontend development server and application build tool.
  • React Router (v7) – Client-side routing and navigation between application pages.
  • Tailwind CSS (v4) – Utility-first CSS framework for responsive interface styling.
  • CSS Variables and Custom Properties – Dynamic styling for dark and light themes and responsive layouts.

UI Components and Data Visualization

  • Lucide React – Icon library for consistent visual interface elements.
  • Radix UI – Accessible, reusable user-interface components.
  • Vaul – Accessible drawer components and interactive modal interfaces.
  • clsx, tailwind-merge, and class-variance-authority (CVA) – Tools for managing conditional CSS classes and reusable component styles.
  • Recharts (v3.8) – Interactive charts for visualizing biometric measurements, sleep patterns, and health trends.
  • SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) – Dynamic graphical representations of simulated ECG and respiratory waveforms.

Backend Development and Cloud Infrastructure

  • Hono (v4) – Lightweight web framework for developing backend API endpoints.
  • Cloudflare Workers – Serverless runtime for backend API processing.
  • Cloudflare – Application hosting and deployment.

Data Management and Development Tools

  • JSON – Structured storage of synthetic astronaut health measurements and mission datasets.
  • Node.js – JavaScript runtime used for development tooling and application build processes.
  • pnpm – Package management and dependency management across the project.
  • Vitest (v3) – Automated unit testing, API validation, and regression testing.
  • GitHub and GitHub Desktop – Version control and collaborative development.

Design and Collaboration

  • Figma – Interface design and user-flow planning.
  • Google Sheets – Health parameter research, monitoring matrices, and calculation documentation.

Research and Scientific Validation

  • NASA Human Research Program resources.
  • NASA-STD-3001.
  • Google Scholar and PubMed.
